column4: The deniers use ضَلَلْنَا for bodies disappearing into earth, making concrete the section's secondary sense of dalal as being present yet lost from sight.
The witness may تَضِلَّ, here forget, and another witness restores what vanished from memory by speaking; this is the section's exact forgetfulness sense of the root.
Moses chooses ضُحًى and the gathering of all the people, so the encounter occurs in the openly visible morning developed in the section.
The earth that covered its occupants تُحَدِّثُ أَخْبَارَهَا, completing the section's movement from what is buried to what is told.
God's favors are explicitly ظَاهِرَةً وَبَاطِنَةً, giving the blessing to be told in 93:11 both its manifest and hidden layers.
God narrates the best account to the Prophet, who had previously been unaware of it, exactly tracing the passage from unknown to revealed and told.
God darkens the night and أَخْرَجَ ضُحَاهَا, literally bringing its morning brightness out after concealment.
Dhu al-Qarnayn finds the sun rising upon a people for whom God made no covering from it, joining وَجَدَهَا with complete exposure to the sun.
A حديث is confided, divulged, disclosed by God, and partly made known by the Prophet; the whole ayah stages speech moving from secrecy to disclosure.
After a killing was concealed, God is مُخْرِجٌ what the people were hiding, a precise instance of the covered fact being brought into view.
What people had been hiding بَدَا لَهُم, directly naming the moment in which the concealed becomes manifest.
The heedless person's covering is removed and sight becomes sharp, giving the image an eschatological instance of cover lifted into perception.
A water drawer brings Joseph out of the well, recognizes him as good news, and the caravan then conceals him as merchandise: finding and re-covering occur in one scene.
Joseph recognizes his brothers while they do not recognize him, concretely showing a known person remaining invisible within ordinary sight.
Joseph privately tells his brother “I am your brother” while his identity remains hidden from the others, making disclosure selective before it becomes public.
The brothers open their baggage and وَجَدُوا their returned goods inside, an exact covered-object-to-found-object movement.
God causes the sleepers to be discovered so that their concealed life becomes public evidence for resurrection.
The thirsty person reaches the apparent water and finds nothing, then وَجَدَ اللَّهَ; the ayah tests sensory finding against what is truly there.
The hoopoe says it has encompassed what Solomon does not know and has brought sure news, moving unseen knowledge into an audible report.
The hoopoe's وَجَدتُّ report identifies the queen, her throne, and her rule, so an act of finding becomes the content of telling.
The hoopoe continues “I found her and her people” and reports their sun worship, carrying the discovered scene fully into speech.
God is described as bringing out الْخَبْءَ, the hidden thing in heaven and earth, while knowing all that people conceal and reveal.
God sends down أَحْسَنَ الْحَدِيثِ and its admonition makes skins tremble and then hearts soften, the Quranic counterpart to speech polishing a heart.
The Prophet did not know the Book or faith, then revelation was made a light by which God guides; it directly fills out “found unaware, then guided.”
After 53:2 denies that the Prophet has strayed, this ayah states that his speech is not from desire, beginning the account of what his telling now is.
The Prophet's utterance is identified as revelation, completing the contrast in 53:2 between being called astray and conveying disclosed guidance.
God promises to make the Prophet recite so that he will not forget, joining received speech to the preservation of what could vanish from memory.
The recitation promise is grounded in God's knowledge of what is public and what is hidden, joining memory, speech, and the visible-hidden pair.
The speakers ask why their companions تُحَدِّثُونَهُم with what God has disclosed to them, explicitly coupling telling with an opening of concealed knowledge.
Enemies sought to يُضِلُّوكَ, but God revealed the Book and taught the Prophet what he did not know, a direct protection-from-error through disclosure.
The Messenger makes clear much that the People of the Book had been concealing, enacting the section's movement from hidden text to public statement.
The revealed Book guides seekers and brings them from darkness into light, completing 5:15's disclosure with the guidance it produces.
The account is news of the unseen revealed to the Prophet, which neither he nor his people knew before; hidden history becomes told knowledge.
The events are called news of the unseen revealed to the Prophet while he was absent from the scene, sharply distinguishing witness from revelation.
The story is news of the unseen revealed to the Prophet, who was not present when the lots were cast or the dispute occurred.
The reports of the messengers are narrated to steady the Prophet's heart, directly supplying the heart-polishing effect the section gives to admonitory speech.
At the meeting of the two seas the fish takes its way into the water, staging a concrete disappearance whose forgetting is named in 18:63.
The servant says he forgot the fish and that it took its way into the sea, bringing forgotten memory and an object vanished in liquid into one scene.
Moses recognizes the lost sign as what they were seeking and retraces the footprints, turning disappearance and forgetting into a search that finds its way back.
Moses and his servant فَوَجَدَا one of God's servants endowed with mercy and hidden knowledge, beginning a lesson in discovery beyond surface sight.
The servant tells Moses not to ask until he يُحْدِثَ له ذكرا, making later speech the appointed means by which concealed meanings will emerge.
At the separation the servant promises to tell the interpretation of events Moses could not patiently grasp, moving seen acts into explained meaning.
The servant finally states the interpretation of the puzzling acts, completing the sequence from visible event to concealed purpose to narration.
Zechariah repeatedly finds provision with Mary and asks its source; her answer attributes the unexpectedly found gift to God.
The record is set down and people وَجَدُوا what they did present before them, so deeds once out of sight become readable and found.
Every soul تَجِدُ its good and evil deeds present, giving intellectual and moral finding an unveiled final form.
God has counted deeds that people forgot and will tell them what they did, so forgotten acts remain preserved for later narration.
A leaf, a grain in earth's darkness, and every moist or dry thing are known and held in a clear record, denying that hiddenness means loss.
After Adam tells the names, God says He knows what the angels reveal and what they conceal, coupling speech with the visible-hidden distinction.
People display parts of the revealed Book and conceal much, while the Prophet is commanded to name God as its revealer; telling answers selective hiding.
Noah says he proclaimed openly and also spoke privately, explicitly setting public telling beside concealed address.
Whether speech is kept secret or voiced aloud, God knows what lies within breasts; neither form of saying escapes the divine hearing.
Those with diseased hearts suppose God will not bring out their concealed rancor, echoing the image of what is inwardly covered being exposed.
God could show the hypocrites so the Prophet would recognize them by marks, and their hidden state is already recognizable in the tone of speech.
On the day people are presented, no hidden thing remains hidden, giving the section's lifting of the cover its absolute boundary.
The person given the record openly calls others to read it, turning the unveiled life of 69:18 into a narrated document.
The day when secrets are tested and exposed gives the section's hidden interior a decisive moment of disclosure.
The earth casts out its burdens before it tells its news in 99:4, supplying the physical uncovering that precedes its speech.
The earth tells because its Lord has inspired it, linking the section's definition of speech received by revelation to 99:4's speaking ground.
The earth casts out what is inside it and becomes empty, a direct reversal of bodies disappearing into the ground in 32:10.
The graves are overturned, making the place of bodily concealment openly yield what it held.
What is in the graves is scattered out, beginning a paired exposure of buried bodies and inner motives.
What is inside breasts is brought out, completing 100:9's movement from physical burial to inward concealment.
A person's record is bound to them and will be brought out on resurrection as an open book, turning stored deeds into visible text.
The person is told to read the disclosed record personally, making the uncovered life speak through its own reader.
The day is sworn by when it جَلَّاهَا, revealing the sun, a direct cosmic image of brightness making visible.
The night is sworn by when it covers the sun, providing the exact concealment paired with 91:3's unveiling.
The night is sworn by when it covers, stating the section's night-as-cover image in the verb يَغْشَىٰ.
The day is sworn by when it becomes manifest, completing 92:1's passage from covering to disclosure.
The Prophet is addressed as the one wrapped in a covering, giving the image a human bearer immediately before the command to speak publicly.
The wrapped Prophet is commanded to rise and warn, enacting movement from covering in 74:1 into proclamation.
The retreating night marks the withdrawal of the cover before the morning appears in the next ayah.
The morning when it shines gives the emergence into visibility that completes 74:33's departing night.
God makes night a garment and sleep a repose, then makes day a rising forth, explicitly staging cover followed by emergence.
The night sign is effaced and the day sign made sight-giving so people can seek bounty and reckon time; obscurity and visibility have distinct work.
Night is made a garment, the Quran's most concrete parallel to the section's opening statement that night is a cover.
One made alive is given light to walk among people, unlike one enclosed in darkness, joining guidance with becoming perceptible within a crowd.
A messenger recites God's clear signs in order to bring believers from darkness into light, so spoken revelation performs the section's uncovering.
The Book is sent to the Prophet to bring people from darkness into light, uniting disclosed speech with divine guidance.
When the throne is made present, Solomon openly identifies it as his Lord's favor and a test of gratitude, enacting speech about a newly manifested gift.
God commands Jesus to remember His favor and then recounts its concrete forms, closely paralleling the command to speak of the Lord's blessing.
Whatever blessing people have is stated to be from God, supplying the attribution implicit in speaking “of your Lord's blessing.”
Moses tells his people to remember God's favor in rescuing them and names the rescue, showing blessing preserved and made public through narration.
The believers are commanded to remember God's favor when He joined once-hostile hearts, a specific hidden transformation recounted as blessing.
The question “Has the حديث of Moses come to you?” exemplifies the section's definition of hadith as speech reaching someone through revelation.
The question whether Moses's حديث has reached the Prophet makes arrival through revealed hearing the point of the wording.
The حديث of Abraham's honored guests is presented as something that has reached the addressee, matching the named dictionary sense exactly.
The حديث of the armies is asked about as revelation that reaches the listener from a past otherwise unseen.
The حديث of the Overwhelming is posed as news that has reached the Prophet, joining future unseen event and present telling.
Destroyed peoples are made أَحَادِيثَ, so vanished communities remain present as stories told by later mouths.
A people scattered and removed from sight are made أَحَادِيثَ, preserving them precisely by turning them into narrated accounts.
The Prophet is commanded to proclaim openly what he has been commanded, giving the section's final telling movement an explicit public stance.
Whoever follows divine guidance will neither يَضِلُّ nor suffer, stating the lasting result of the guidance that follows dāll in 93:7.
The Prophet says that if he strays it is his own loss, but if he is guided it is through what his Lord reveals; revelation is the audible source of guidance.
God does not let a people stray after guiding them until He makes clear what they must avoid, so clarification guards guidance from loss.
The opponents have strayed and therefore cannot find a way, placing loss of direction and inability to find in the same consequence.
The opponents have strayed and cannot find a path, a concise inverse of being found in a state of dalal and then guided.
Moses describes his earlier act as done while he was among the ضَالِّينَ, placing a confessed former state immediately before divine commissioning.
Moses says his Lord then granted judgment and made him a messenger, completing 26:20's movement from error or unawareness into guided speech.
The condemned وَجَدُوا their fathers ضَالِّينَ, bringing “finding” and “astray” together while showing discovery that merely perpetuates inherited error.
God distinguishes messengers whose stories were told to the Prophet from messengers not told before, marking narration's boundary against the still unspoken.
As in 4:164, some messengers have been narrated to the Prophet and others have not, preserving both the disclosed account and what remains covered.
God says He narrates reports of what preceded and has given the Prophet a remembrance, making the hidden past into present admonition.
God narrates the sleepers' news in truth, turning their secluded and disputed history into sure revealed knowledge.
The prophetic accounts are not a fabricated حديث but confirmation and detailed guidance, defining told history as revelatory rather than invented speech.
God knows the unseen and does not disclose His unseen to anyone, stating the veil before the exception in 72:27.
A chosen messenger is the exception to concealed unseen knowledge, establishing revelation as authorized disclosure.
The guarded disclosure ensures that the messengers have conveyed their Lord's messages, carrying hidden knowledge through to public delivery.
The Prophet does not withhold the unseen, so what God discloses is not kept under a cover but conveyed.
God does not disclose the unseen indiscriminately but chooses messengers, clarifying who can carry covered knowledge into speech.
God's speech reaches a human by revelation, from behind a veil, or through a messenger, exactly mapping hearing and revelation across a boundary of concealment.
The Reminder is sent down so the Prophet may make clear to people what was revealed, making explanation the final stage of reception.
God takes responsibility for gathering the revelation and its recitation, securing the words before they are publicly voiced.
Once God recites the revelation, the Prophet is told to follow its recitation, tracing speech from divine delivery into human reception.
God also takes responsibility for its clarification, completing collection and recitation with the making-clear central to this image.
God teaches by the pen, naming a medium by which knowledge moves from the unseen or unknown into a communicable mark.
God teaches the human being what he did not know, the same transition from unawareness to received knowledge used in the section.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best are the ones God guides, coupling audible words with the guidance that follows finding.
The revelation is a reminder for one with a receptive heart who listens as a witness, matching speech that reaches the ear and works upon the heart.
A group of jinn listens to the Quran, tells one another to attend, then returns to warn its people; heard revelation becomes retold warning.
The jinn identify what they heard as a Book guiding to truth and a straight path, stating the guidance produced by the speech in 46:29.
The Prophet is told that jinn listened and then reported the wondrous Quran, another complete reception-to-telling movement.
The Arabic Quran varies warnings so that it may يُحْدِثُ لَهُمْ ذِكْرًا, linking the h-d-th root to speech bringing remembrance into being.
Each newly given reminder is heard while the people play, showing revealed speech arriving at ears but failing to open attention.
Each newly given reminder is met by turning away, a precise contrast to admonitory حديث polishing a receptive heart.
God covers the sleepers' ears in the cave for years, making concealment operate through hearing itself.
God raises the sleepers in order to make known which party best counted the time, turning covered sleep into disclosed knowledge.
The sun skirts the cave that conceals the sleepers, and the ayah immediately states that whom God guides is guided and whom He lets stray finds no directing protector.
The awakened sleepers send one companion out discreetly and tell him not to make anyone aware of them, explicitly trying to remain hidden before 18:21's discovery.
The ayah directly compares making charity visible with concealing it while giving to the poor, a concrete moral use of open and covered action.
One endowed with good provision spends from it secretly and openly, joining bestowed favor with its hidden and manifest expression.
God “does not go astray and does not forget,” placing the section's two senses of d-l-l at a deliberate divine limit.
The oath denies that “your companion” has strayed, illuminating 93:7 by distinguishing the Prophet's earlier dāll state from his present truthful mission.
One led astray despite knowledge has hearing and heart sealed and sight veiled, reversing the section's finding, guidance, and lifting of cover.
Layered sea, wave, cloud, and darkness make even one's hand nearly invisible; without God's light there is no light, the full negative of morning disclosure.
On judgment day the rejecters cannot conceal any حديث from God, setting an absolute boundary on keeping speech hidden.
Mixing truth with falsehood and then concealing it makes disclosed truth disappear within another substance, close to the section's water-in-milk figure.
The People of the Book are charged with clothing truth in falsehood and knowingly concealing it, repeating the image of discernible truth covered by mixture.
Those who conceal clear proofs and guidance after God has made them clear reverse the section's movement from found guidance into telling.
The covenant requires the Book to be made clear and not concealed, directly marking concealment as the breach of revelatory speech.
Noah's people put fingers in ears and wrap themselves in garments to avoid his call, physically blocking the speech that should reach and uncover.
The hearers claim covers over hearts, heaviness in ears, and a veil between themselves and the Prophet, the opposite of speech reaching and polishing a heart.
Those reminded forget what they sent ahead while covers lie over their hearts and heaviness in their ears, binding forgetting, covering, and refusal of guidance.
Eyes are under a covering from God's remembrance and ears cannot hear, making concealment a chosen failure of both perception and reception.
When the Prophet recites the Quran, a concealed veil stands between him and those who deny the hereafter, preventing disclosed speech from being received.
A rust-like covering has accumulated on hearts through deeds, directly opposing the section's image of admonition polishing a heart clean.
The question about pondering the Quran locates locks upon hearts, presenting speech whose clarifying work is stopped by an inner closure.
Idle حديث is purchased to mislead people from God's way, reversing the section's حديث that discloses, admonishes, and guides.
People recognize God's blessing and then deny it, the direct failure to move from a found favor into grateful acknowledgment.
Those who conceal what God sent down in the Book sell disclosure for gain, the opposite stance to speaking openly of divine gift.
The Prophet is told to state that he does not possess God's treasures or know the unseen, defining the boundary between the messenger and what remains concealed unless revealed.
The rejecters tell one another not to listen to the Quran and to drown it in noise, deliberately preventing revelation from reaching the ear as meaningful speech.
Adam is promised that in the garden he will not تَضْحَىٰ, be exposed to the sun; this negative use clarifies the dictionary sense of going out into sunlight.
Punishment may come at ضُحًى while a town is playing, using the morning as the exposed public hour rather than the cover of night.
The oath by the sun and ضُحَاهَا ties duha directly to the sun's spreading brightness.
The night is sworn by as it withdraws, an alternate formulation of the cover beginning to lift.
The dawn is sworn by as it breathes, completing 81:17 with light's gradual emergence.
God splits the dawn and makes night for repose, placing opening light beside settled darkness.
Night is wrapped over day and day over night, portraying concealment and disclosure as reciprocal coverings.
Night covers day and pursues it swiftly, giving the section's night-cover a cosmic action.
God covers day with night in a context of signs made distinct for reflection, supporting the cover-and-recognition relation.
Day is stripped away and people are suddenly in darkness, showing visibility itself as a layer that can be removed.
The thought experiment of perpetual night asks who besides God could bring light, making emergence from cover depend wholly on Him.
The matching thought experiment asks who could bring night for rest if day were perpetual, preserving the purpose of the cover as well as its lifting.
God's mercy supplies both resting night and sight-giving day, completing the visible-hidden pair with their human uses.
Night is made for rest and day sight-giving, a compact functional parallel to night covering and duha revealing.
God makes night for rest and day مُبْصِرًا, giving the day the quality of making sight possible.
Night is made for rest and day for seeing, repeating the image as a provision people are asked to recognize.
Day is made for livelihood, giving the uncovered interval in 78:10-11 its outward human work.
Joseph orders the brothers' goods hidden in their baggage so they may recognize them later, supplying the concealment that 12:65 resolves by opening and finding.
The brothers themselves define the penalty by the person in whose baggage the cup is found, making discovery of the hidden object decisive.
The bags are searched and the cup is brought out of the brother's container, physically completing concealment, search, and extraction.
Joseph asks to be mentioned to the king, but the freed prisoner forgets the mention, so failed memory keeps Joseph covered in prison.
After a period the former prisoner remembers and announces that he can report the dream's interpretation, allowing forgotten Joseph to re-enter public speech.
Joseph keeps the brothers' accusation within himself and does not reveal it, a deliberate pause between hidden knowledge and later disclosure.
Joseph's question about the brothers' former act prompts recognition, initiating the disclosure of the person who has stood unrecognized before them.
The brothers ask whether he is Joseph and he answers that he is, completing hidden identity with explicit self-naming.
Jacob says he can detect Joseph's scent before the caravan arrives, extending the section's sensory finding beyond sight.
When the shirt is placed on Jacob's face, his sight returns, turning an indirect sensory recognition into restored visibility.
Dhu al-Qarnayn finds the sun setting and finds a people beside its setting place, a repeated sensory use of وَجَدَ framed by sunlight.
He finds a people who can scarcely understand speech, pairing physical finding with the boundary at which words fail to reach understanding.
Moses's mother receives revelation to cast the child into the river and a promise that God will return him, beginning a hidden-child-to-restoration sequence.
Pharaoh's household picks the concealed infant from the river, a discovery whose true identity remains unknown to the finders.
Moses's mother nearly discloses his identity, but God steadies her heart so the secret remains covered for a time.
Moses's sister watches him from a distance while his captors remain unaware of her, staging observation hidden within a crowd.
The sister offers to guide the household to carers while concealing that she is guiding them back to Moses's own family.
God returns Moses to his mother so she will know the promise is true, ending concealed separation in recognition and knowledge.
The Prophet was not present when Moses received the command, so the narrated scene marks knowledge supplied without ordinary witnessing.
Generations and distance separate the Prophet from Midian, sharpening the hidden historical gap that revelation crosses.
The Prophet was not beside the mount but is sent as mercy to warn, completing absence from the event with public speech about it.
Mary takes a screen from her people and the spirit then appears to her as a man, a literal covered space followed by manifestation.
The command not to reveal hidden adornment even guards against a footfall that would make it known, showing concealment undone through hearing.
God knows the stealthy glance and what breasts conceal, making even the nearly invisible act perceptible to divine knowledge.
People could not hide from their own hearing, sight, and skins bearing witness, so the senses that once received actions become their narrators.
Secret speech and private counsel are heard and recorded, so words do not cease to exist merely because human ears are excluded.
God is present with every private conversation and will later tell its speakers what they did, joining hidden speech to eventual disclosure.
Secretly conveying affection is set beside God's knowledge of what is concealed and declared, making private communication itself visible to Him.
Whether people reveal what is within themselves or conceal it, God calls it to account, giving inward hiddenness a future public consequence.
The Prophet is told to say that God knows what people hide in their breasts and what they reveal, placing the visible-hidden pair in proclamation.
God knows speech spoken aloud and what people conceal, covering both audible expression and its unvoiced counterpart.
The Prophet is comforted that God knows what opponents conceal and reveal, so hostile speech and its hidden source are both already perceived.
God may يُحْدِثُ after a divorce some new matter, preserving the h-d-th root's sense of bringing something previously absent into being.
Believers are told to spend God's provision secretly and openly, another concrete act performed under cover and before view.
Those who recite the Book also spend provision secretly and openly, placing heard or spoken revelation beside both modes of action.
The people of Paradise say they found their Lord's promise true and ask the people of Fire whether they found the same, making future promise present verification.
God says وَجَدْنَاهُ صَابِرًا of Job, illustrating intellectual or evaluative finding rather than the section's sensory finding.
The Prophet is told to say he does not find in what was revealed a forbidden food beyond those named, showing finding as discernment within received speech.
Whatever good people send ahead they will find with God, treating unseen preserved action as something later encountered.
Believers are told to remember God's favor when unseen forces turned back attacking armies, making hidden aid a narrated blessing.
God's favors cannot be fully counted, marking a limit on the command to tell blessing without denying the duty to recognize its source.
The phrase “by your Lord's blessing” publicly rejects the charge of madness against the Prophet, making divine favor part of his spoken vindication.
The Prophet is commanded to remind, and “by your Lord's blessing” he is neither soothsayer nor madman; favor supports the stance of open proclamation.
Immediately after the revealed “حديث of Moses,” Moses sees a fire, tells his family what he has perceived, and hopes to bring news or find guidance there; sight, telling, and finding converge.
When God's signs are recited, believers' hearts tremble and their faith increases, a direct Quranic instance of heard admonition acting upon the heart.
Those given knowledge recognize the revelation as truth, believe it, and their hearts humbly submit, showing disclosed speech polishing inward perception.
Protection is granted so an outsider may hear the speech of God, making the arrival of revealed words through hearing the ayah's decisive act.
Listeners are commanded to attend silently when the Quran is recited, stating the receptive posture by which revealed speech reaches them.
Hatred has appeared from opponents' mouths while what their breasts conceal is greater, sharply separating audible disclosure from a deeper hidden interior.
People say with their mouths what is not in their hearts, while God knows what they conceal; spoken appearance and hidden reality diverge.
Satan whispers in order to reveal to Adam and his wife what had been concealed from them of their nakedness, making disclosure itself the temptation's aim.
Their nakedness becomes visible and they begin covering themselves with garden leaves, staging exposure followed immediately by an improvised veil.
After eating from the tree, Adam and his wife's nakedness becomes visible and they patch leaves over themselves, repeating the exact uncovering-and-covering movement.
People are commanded to remember God's favor and asked whether any creator besides Him provides for them, joining recollection of blessing to public attribution of its source.
Abraham is grateful for God's favors, and God chooses and guides him to a straight path; favor, acknowledgment, and guidance meet in one description.
Solomon voices a prayer to be enabled to thank the favor bestowed on him and his parents, exemplifying blessing deliberately brought into speech.
The condemned faces are described as though covered with pieces of dark night, making night-covering a visible human condition.
The deniers ask whether return is possible after death and becoming dust; 50:4 answers this disappearance by affirming that God knows what earth diminishes.
A blast sounds and the dead rush from their graves to their Lord, turning concealed bodies into an openly moving multitude.
Human beings come from earth, return into it, and are brought out from it again, explicitly denying that burial is final disappearance.
The records are spread open, making what was stored and closed available to sight.
After the records are opened, every soul knows what it has brought, giving disclosure its corresponding act of recognition.
The human being is informed that day of what was sent ahead and left behind, turning a completed but hidden life into narrated knowledge.
What the idolaters fabricated ضَلَّ عَنْهُمْ, vanishes from them, using the section's root in its concrete sense of something once asserted becoming lost from view.
At fulfillment of the warning, what the rejecters fabricated has vanished from them, another direct use of d-l-l for disappearance rather than wayward travel.
At judgment every soul encounters what it sent ahead and false objects of worship vanish from their devotees, joining rediscovery of deeds to disappearance of inventions.
What the self-wrongers invented has vanished from them, preserving the root's “gone missing” face in an eschatological scene.
On judgment day the false objects that people invented vanish from them, so hidden reality displaces their lost fabrication.
When witnesses are summoned and proof demanded, the fabricated partners vanish from their worshippers, making failed finding expose the false claim.
The condemned answer that the objects they invoked have vanished from them, a first-person acknowledgment of the root's disappearance sense.
The People of Scripture find the unlettered Messenger written in the Torah and Gospel, turning a preserved textual sign into present recognition.
Moses finds a crowd watering and notices two women held back from it, a gaze that singles out otherwise overlooked people within the crowd.
The infant Moses is placed in a chest and cast into the river to be taken by an enemy, a concealed child carried into an unknowing finder's hands.
Moses's sister guides the household to a nurse, God returns him to his mother, and later brings him out of distress; hidden identity and guidance restore what was lost.
Solomon's death remains hidden from the jinn until the staff gives way and his fall makes it clear, a physical fact moving from concealment to discovery.
While the Prophet recites and people act, not even an atom is hidden from God and all is in a clear record, coupling utterance, perception, and preserved disclosure.
God is named both the Manifest and the Hidden, placing the section's visible-hidden polarity in a single divine description.
The Messenger's duty is clear conveyance, while God knows what people reveal and conceal; public telling stands against complete divine knowledge of both states.
The Prophet has seen the messenger on the clear horizon, supplying the act of visible perception before 81:24 says he does not withhold the unseen.
After the covered Prophet is told to rise and warn, he is commanded to magnify his Lord, specifying the God-directed content of the public utterance.
The Prophet is addressed as the one wrapped up, placing him literally beneath a cover before the ensuing night recitation.
The wrapped Prophet is commanded to stand through the night, moving from covered rest into alert reception.
He is commanded to recite the Quran in measured form, completing the movement from wrapping and night into articulated revelation.
The Prophet is commanded to recite in his Lord's name, making received knowledge cross immediately into spoken proclamation.
The trustworthy Spirit brings the revelation down, identifying the messenger by which concealed divine speech reaches the human sphere.
The revelation descends upon the Prophet's heart so that he may warn, joining inward reception to outward address.
The disclosure is in a clear Arabic tongue, giving audible and intelligible form to what descended upon the heart.
Gabriel brings the Quran down upon the Prophet's heart as confirmation and guidance, a precise revealed-speech-to-guided-heart sequence.
The Holy Spirit brings the Quran from the Lord to steady believers and make it guidance and good news, spelling out what the conveyed word does within its hearers.
God sends the clarifying Book down during a blessed night as warning, making the night-cover itself the setting from which revelation emerges.
A breast opened to Islam follows light from the Lord, while hardened hearts resist remembrance; openness and light oppose the unpolished heart.
Hearts become hard after the signs, even harder than stone, reversing the section's account of admonition polishing and opening hearts.
Broken covenant leads to hardened hearts and distortion of revealed words, joining inner corrosion to speech prevented from disclosing truth faithfully.
The ayah says that eyes are not what go blind but hearts within breasts, setting a boundary between surface visibility and genuine perception.
The people of the Fire admit that listening or reasoning would have saved them, identifying failed reception of warning as their decisive loss.
Believers are warned not to imitate those who say “we hear” while they do not hear, distinguishing audible arrival from inward reception.
After God's signs are recited, the question asks what حديث people will believe after God and His signs, setting revealed discourse as the limit beyond which substitute speech cannot guide.
The question asks what حديث after this revelation the rejecters will believe, exposing refusal at the final point where clarifying speech has reached them.
The hearers are challenged for treating “this حديث” with disdain, contrasting the revealed word's arrival with a response that suppresses its worth.
People know only the outward surface of worldly life while remaining heedless of the hereafter, showing manifest knowledge that still conceals the larger reality.
God promises never to let the slain believers' deeds be lost, setting a divine boundary against the d-l-l sense of disappearance.
The Prophet cannot make those in graves hear, marking the human limit of speech reaching what the earth covers.
Noah is commanded to deny possessing God's treasures or knowing the unseen, preserving the boundary between prophetic telling and unrevealed hidden knowledge.
